title: The First Movement
reflection:
The Examen begins with a simple act: becoming aware. Before anything is examined or offered, there must be a moment of stillness — a turning of attention toward what is actually present.

Today your body begins its release. Ignatius would ask: where have you sensed God in the past day? In the heaviness, in the ache, in the slowing — there is data. Begin there.
closing: Lord, sharpen my awareness. Let me not miss what you are doing in the ordinary moments of this day. Amen.

scripture.text: Be still, and know that I am God.

title: Gratitude as Foundation
reflection:
The first movement of the Examen is gratitude — not forced thankfulness, but honest noticing of what has been given. Even on the heaviest days, something has been received.

What, today, can you name as gift? It may be small. A warmth. A breath. A person. Name it before God, unhurriedly.
closing: For what I have received and not noticed — thank you. Open my eyes to gift. Amen.

scripture.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his love endures forever.

title: Asking for Light
reflection:
The second movement of the Examen is petition: asking God to illuminate the review of your day. This is not self-examination by willpower alone. It is an invitation to see alongside Another.

Before you look back over the past days, ask: show me what I need to see. Not everything — just what is useful. Trust that the Spirit will highlight what matters.
closing: Illuminate my review. Show me what is mine to see. I do not need to see everything — only what you want me to notice. Amen.

scripture.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

title: Reviewing the Day
reflection:
Move slowly through the past day. Not to judge — but to notice. Where did energy flow freely? Where did it tighten or drain? The body in its limits is an honest reporter.

Ignatius taught that consolation and desolation are readable signs. What did you feel most today? Least? What were you drawn toward? What did you avoid?
closing: I review this day with curiosity, not judgment. Thank you for being in it with me. Amen.

scripture.text: Search me, O God, and know my heart.

title: Facing What Is True
reflection:
The Examen does not ask for a curated account. It asks for an honest one. Where did you act from fear rather than love? Where did you contract when you might have opened?

This is not the moment for self-condemnation. It is the moment for clarity. What is true today? Say it, quietly, to the One who already knows.
closing: I name what is true without hiding. You have seen it all. Receive my honesty as a form of prayer. Amen.

scripture.text: The truth will set you free.

title: Consolation
reflection:
Ignatius defined consolation as any interior movement that draws us toward God — an increase of faith, hope, love; a quiet joy; a sense of rightness. It does not require feeling good.

Look back: was there a moment of consolation in the past day, however brief? A moment of connection, clarity, or peace? Receive it as sign — not of your merit, but of God's presence.
closing: Thank you for the consolations I almost missed. Teach me to receive them more fully. Amen.

scripture.text: As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you.

title: Desolation
reflection:
Desolation is the interior movement away from God — heaviness, dryness, agitation, a sense of distance. Ignatius said: in desolation, do not change course. Stay. Endure. Trust the structure of your commitments.

If this day has been desolate, that is not failure. Desolation has its own instruction. What has it revealed about what you are attached to? What have you learned from the absence?
closing: In the desolation, you are still here. I stay. I trust the ground beneath the feeling. Amen.

scripture.text: Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.

title: Rules for Discernment
reflection:
Ignatius gave his companions rules for discernment — not rigid laws, but patterns to recognise. One pattern: the enemy attacks at the weak point. In consolation, we grow careless; in desolation, we despair. Neither is the whole truth.

As energy returns in this phase, notice: where does carelessness tempt you? What assumptions come easily when things feel well?
closing: Keep me attentive even in the lightness. Let consolation deepen me rather than soften my attention. Amen.

scripture.text: Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.

title: Holy Desire
reflection:
Ignatius believed that our deepest desires — the ones beneath our surface wants — are the fingerprints of God. To ask "what do I truly want?" is a spiritual question, not merely a psychological one.

In this lighter season, what is rising in you? Not what you think you should want. What genuinely stirs? Name it as an honest prayer.
closing: This is what I desire: [name it]. I bring it to you. Purify it, if it needs purifying. Receive it, if it is yours. Amen.

scripture.text: Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart.

title: Freedom
reflection:
The Ignatian tradition prizes interior freedom — the capacity to choose from love rather than fear, from genuine preference rather than compulsion. Not indifference to all things, but freedom within all things.

Where are you not free today? What choice feels driven by fear, habit, or the need for approval? Name it. Then ask: what would love choose?
closing: Free me from what is not truly mine to carry. Let me choose today from love. Amen.

scripture.text: I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content.

title: Finding God in All Things
reflection:
The great Ignatian conviction: God can be found in all things. Not just in prayer, church, or solitude — but in the texture of an ordinary day. In a conversation, a task, a body doing its work.

As creativity rises in you this week, where might the sacred be hiding in the ordinary? What would you notice if you were looking for God in the mundane?
closing: Open my eyes to where you already are. Let me not look past you in search of something more impressive. Amen.

scripture.text: Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

title: The Election
reflection:
The climax of the Spiritual Exercises is the Election — a choice made from a place of interior freedom, in consolation, for the greater good. Not every day contains a formal election, but every day contains smaller versions of this practice.

What choice is before you today? Can you bring it to a moment of stillness, invite God's perspective, and choose from there rather than from anxiety?
closing: I bring this choice to you. I want to choose well. Guide the movement. Amen.

scripture.text: I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.

title: Contemplation to Attain Love
reflection:
The final meditation of the Exercises: love shows itself more in deeds than in words. And all gifts return to the Giver. Ignatius invites us to see everything we have — talent, energy, relationship — as on loan, to be received gratefully and used generously.

What have you been given this cycle? What are you being asked to give back?
closing: Take, Lord, and receive all I have. All is yours. Do with it what you will. Amen.

scripture.text: Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.

title: Sent
reflection:
Ignatius did not train contemplatives to stay in cells. He trained companions to go out — to carry what they had received into the world, in service of the greater good.

At this fullest point of your cycle, what are you being sent to do? Not heroically. Simply: where does your presence, your care, your attention serve something beyond yourself today?
closing: I am sent. Show me where. Let me go willingly. Amen.

scripture.text: God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God.

title: Companions on the Way
reflection:
Ignatius wrote for a community — the Society of Jesus. The Exercises were meant to be made in company with a director, and the life that followed was meant to be lived with companions.

Who are your companions on this way? Who keeps you honest, challenges your consolations, sits with your desolations? Offer gratitude for them today.
closing: Thank you for those who walk with me. Let me also be that for someone else. Amen.

scripture.text: Where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them.

title: Magis
reflection:
The Jesuit motto: ad maiorem Dei gloriam — for the greater glory of God. And the animating question behind it: not "what is enough" but "what is more?" Not more effort, but more love. More attention. More presence.

What would "more" look like today — not in quantity, but in quality of attention and care?
closing: For your greater glory. Not my reputation, not my comfort — your glory. Let that be the measure. Amen.

scripture.text: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.

title: The Long Gaze
reflection:
Ignatian contemplation involves holding a scene — from Scripture, from life — and simply looking. Not analysing. Not extracting lessons. Just looking, long and quietly, until something stirs.

As this outward season turns, take a long gaze at your own life. What do you see when you are not rushing past it?
closing: I look at my life without flinching. You are in it. That is enough. Amen.

scripture.text: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.

title: The Inward Journey
reflection:
The Exercises move from active engagement with God's story outward to the deep interior — from the Incarnation to the Passion, from fullness to stripping. This mirrors your cycle's movement now.

What is being stripped in you? Not taken maliciously — but cleared. What becomes visible when the busyness recedes?
closing: Strip away what is not essential. I am willing to be simplified. Amen.

scripture.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

title: Consolation Without Cause
reflection:
Ignatius distinguished consolation with cause (arising from something specific) from consolation without cause — a pure gift, arising from nowhere, given by God alone.

Have you received any consolation recently that had no apparent reason? A surge of peace, gratitude, or love that arrived unasked? This is grace operating at its most direct. Receive it.
closing: For the consolations I did not earn and cannot explain — thank you. Teach me to receive freely. Amen.

scripture.text: For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith.

title: The Dark Night
reflection:
John of the Cross, companion in spirit to Ignatius, spoke of the dark night — not as punishment, but as the soul's deeper purification. When the light of consolation is withdrawn, what remains?

In this inward season, what is being asked of you that you cannot do with your own resources? That insufficiency is not weakness. It is the doorway.
closing: I cannot do this alone. I was never meant to. I wait for your sufficiency to meet my lack. Amen.

scripture.text: Even the darkness will not be dark to you; the night will shine like the day.

title: Weekly Examen
reflection:
Take the full Examen today. Move through all five movements: gratitude, petition for light, review of the week, response to what you find, and renewal of intention.

Do not rush. Give each movement its time. This is a week's worth of living — it deserves more than a moment's attention.
closing: I have reviewed this week honestly. I receive your forgiveness where I fell short. I renew my intention to go forward with more love. Amen.

scripture.text: Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.

title: Spiritual Poverty
reflection:
The first beatitude in Ignatius's world: blessed are the poor in spirit. Not material poverty necessarily, but interior poverty — the willingness to hold things lightly, to not cling.

What are you clinging to today? What would it feel like to hold it with an open hand rather than a closed fist?
closing: I am holding too tightly. Show me what to release. Give me the grace of open hands. Amen.

scripture.text: For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.

title: Agere Contra
reflection:
Ignatius taught agere contra — acting against one's disordered inclinations. Not self-punishment, but a deliberate movement against what pulls us away from our better selves.

What does your desolation incline you toward today? Withdrawal? Harshness? Numbness? Make one small counter-movement. Not heroic — just one degree in the opposite direction.
closing: Against the pull of this desolation, I choose one small act of faithfulness. That is enough. Amen.

scripture.text: We also glory in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance.

title: The Hidden Life
reflection:
Most of Jesus's life was hidden — thirty years in Nazareth, unremarkable, unrecorded. Ignatius meditated on this: that God chose obscurity, ordinary work, dailiness.

Your hidden faithfulness — the small choices no one will see — may be where the most important work of your life is happening. What is your Nazareth today?
closing: Let my hiddenness be holy. Let me serve faithfully in the unremarkable. That is enough. Amen.

scripture.text: Oh, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!

title: Sorrow with Christ
reflection:
In the Third Week of the Exercises, Ignatius asks us to feel with Christ in his suffering — not as observers, but as companions. This is the grace of the luteal season: a thinning of the boundary between our experience and the experience of others.

Where is there suffering in your immediate world today? Can you be present to it — not to fix it, but to accompany it?
closing: I accompany what suffers. I do not look away. Let my presence be a small act of love. Amen.

scripture.text: Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.

title: Poverty of Spirit, Again
reflection:
Ignatius returned again and again to the same themes — because the spiritual life does not progress linearly. We revisit the same lessons at deeper levels, each cycle revealing what the last could not.

What is this cycle teaching you about simplicity? About what you actually need versus what you thought you needed?
closing: Teach me again what I learned before, more deeply this time. I am still learning. Amen.

scripture.text: Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances.

title: The Third Kind of Humility
reflection:
Ignatius described three kinds of humility. The third — the most radical — is the desire not merely to follow God's will, but to identify with the poor and lowly Christ, choosing poverty over wealth when both are equal in God's service.

Where in your life is a costly choice available to you? You do not have to make it today. But name it. Know it is there.
closing: I am not yet ready for the third kind. But I want to want it. Begin that work in me. Amen.

scripture.text: I press on toward the goal to win the prize for which God has called me.

title: Contemplata Aliis Tradere
reflection:
"To give to others what one has contemplated" — the Dominican phrase that shaped Jesuit spirituality. What you have received is not for keeping. It is for passing on.

What have you received in this cycle — in this phase, in these days of prayer — that is meant to be given? Who needs what you have been given?
closing: What I have received, I hold on behalf of others. Show me to whom I am to give it. Amen.

scripture.text: It is finished.

title: Waiting in Trust
reflection:
The Ignatian tradition does not rush resolution. Discernment takes time. Some decisions must be lived with before they can be made. Waiting is not inaction — it is a form of fidelity.

What are you waiting for clarity on? Can you trust that the waiting itself is part of the answer?
closing: I wait without forcing. The answer will come in your time. I am learning to trust the waiting. Amen.

scripture.text: But they who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength.

title: Confirmation
reflection:
Ignatius wrote that a decision made in consolation, confirmed over time, carries particular authority. The confirmation is not a single moment — it is a pattern that persists across moods and seasons.

What has remained constant for you across this cycle — despite the changes in energy, mood, and clarity? That persistence may be confirmation of something true.
closing: What has persisted despite the seasons — I receive as confirmed. I will act on what has been shown. Amen.

scripture.text: Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

title: The Body as Companion
reflection:
Ignatius was a wounded soldier — his spirituality was shaped by a body that had known injury, convalescence, and slow recovery. He did not distrust the body; he read it.

Your body in this extended waiting phase is communicating something. Not just biologically — spiritually. What is it saying? Can you listen without judgment?
closing: My body is your instrument too. Teach me to read it wisely and to treat it with the dignity it deserves. Amen.

scripture.text: The Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for.

title: Preparation and Providence
reflection:
Ignatius said: pray as if everything depends on God; act as if everything depends on you. This is not contradiction — it is the tension that produces faithful action.

In this waiting, what is yours to do? And what must you leave to providence? Draw that line today as honestly as you can.
closing: I do what is mine to do. I release what is not. I trust your providence with the rest. Amen.

scripture.text: I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans to prosper you.

title: Perseverance
reflection:
The Exercises take thirty days. Most of the growth happens in the middle — when the novelty has worn off and the end is not yet in sight. This is the zone of perseverance.

You are in your own long middle. What keeps you faithful when the felt sense of God's presence is thin? That answer is worth knowing.
closing: I continue. Not because I feel certain, but because this is the direction I have chosen. Hold me to it. Amen.

scripture.text: Let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us.

title: Cura Personalis
reflection:
The Jesuit tradition insists on cura personalis — care for the whole person, in their particularity. Not a generic spirituality, but one fitted to who you actually are.

How are you caring for yourself as a whole person in this season? Not just spiritually — physically, emotionally, relationally. What needs tending that you have been neglecting?
closing: I am a whole person. Help me tend all of what I am, not only the parts that seem spiritual. Amen.

scripture.text: Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.

title: Ad Majorem
reflection:
Return to the question of purpose. Not career or life-plan — but the deeper question: for what are you here? What is the greater glory you are oriented toward, even when you cannot see it?

Ignatius trained people to keep this horizon in view, especially when the immediate circumstances were unclear. Keep your horizon in view today.
closing: For your greater glory — not my comfort, not my reputation. Let that remain the direction. Amen.

scripture.text: Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord.

title: Grace Upon Grace
reflection:
Ignatius believed that grace builds on grace — that what God has done in us previously is the foundation for what God will do next. No grace is wasted. No good season is erased by a difficult one.

Look back across this cycle. Where has grace built on grace? What has grown that you did not plant?
closing: Grace upon grace. I receive the inheritance of what you have already done. Amen.

scripture.text: No one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

title: The New Beginning
reflection:
The Exercises end not with achievement but with a renewed orientation — a person more free, more loving, more available to God and to the world. The end is not a conclusion but a sending.

As this cycle nears its close, what is the renewed orientation you are carrying? What is different in you from when you began?
closing: I am being sent again. Renewed, not perfected. Willing, not certain. Ready. Amen.

scripture.text: Eye has not seen, nor ear heard the things which God has prepared for those who love him.

title: Return and Receive
reflection:
The pilgrim returns — not to the same place they left, but to a familiar place that now looks different because they have changed.

You have completed another cycle of prayer and embodied living. You are not the same person who began it. Return now to the beginning with everything you have received. The next cycle will meet you there.
closing: I return changed. I receive the new cycle as gift. Begin again in me what only you can begin. Amen.

scripture.text: See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it?
